title: The counterintuitive way spacecraft catch the space station
one_idea: To catch something in orbit, you slow down and drop into a lower orbit — a lower orbit is faster, so you catch up.

analogy.source_term: To catch something in orbit, you slow down and drop into a lower orbit; a lower orbit is faster, so you close the gap.
mapping: Dragon spacecraft trying to catch the ISS
a delivery truck trying to catch another truck on the same circular road
Both spacecraft moving at thousands of miles per hour in orbit
both trucks driving at the same speed on the same road
Dropping to a lower orbit to catch up faster
the chasing truck taking an inner lane, which has a shorter path and a higher speed
analogy.limitation: Unlike trucks on a road, spacecraft in orbit are continuously falling around Earth — there is no road surface, just gravity.

audience_misconception: You should fly faster to catch the space station. In orbit, both objects are already moving at thousands of miles per hour; flying faster only raises your orbit and makes you move slower relative to the target.

claims.claim: SpaceX Crew-13 arrived at the International Space Station in under 8 hours using standard orbital rendezvous procedures.
The ISS orbits Earth at approximately 17,500 miles per hour at an altitude of roughly 250 miles.
A spacecraft must match both the altitude and phase of the target orbit to dock; flying faster raises the orbit and does not close the gap.

concepts.name: orbital rendezvous
concepts.definition: The process of bringing two orbiting spacecraft together so they can dock, requiring matched altitude, matched speed, and correct phase position.

concepts.name: orbit
concepts.definition: An object in orbit is constantly falling around a planet. The higher the orbit, the slower the orbital speed. The lower the orbit, the faster the speed.

concepts.name: orbital phasing
concepts.definition: Adjusting your orbit so that you arrive at the same point as the target at the same time, by raising or lowering your orbit to change your relative speed.

loops.question: If the space station is so fast, why can't you just fly faster to reach it?

news_hook.event: SpaceX Crew-13 docked with the International Space Station in under 8 hours after launch, using standard orbital rendezvous procedures.

original_contribution: Explains the counterintuitive orbital phasing technique — that you must slow down to catch up — and connects it to the Crew-13 mission in plain terms without jargon.
